extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers of anthropology and humor studies; practitioners interested in cross-cultural humor
extracted.subtask_description: Use anthropological criteria to evaluate or produce humor with sensitivity to cross-cultural universals and variation, focusing on occasion, relationships, targets, modes, functions, and theoretical fit. Emphasizes that funniness is situated in audience, context, and cultural taxonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural license (occasion-based permissibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: All cultures have specific occasions where humor is expected and specific occasions where humor is forbidden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the humor occurs at an occasion that culturally permits joking (festivals, rites of passage, particular conversational phases) or at an occasion that forbids it (mourning, sacred rituals, interactions with formal authority). The occasion can determine acceptability regardless of content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joking relationships (formalized speaker-target dyads)
rubrics_metrics.description: All cultures have 'joking relationships'—formalized dyads (often kin-based) where mutual joking is socially required; failure to joke can itself be a violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the speaker and target are in a culturally recognized joking relationship (e.g., cross-cousin, brother-/sister-in-law, grandparent-grandchild, tribal-pair). If so, humor that might be taboo elsewhere can be obligatory and acceptable; if not, similar jokes may be transgressive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Different cultures designate different legitimate targets for humor (ethnic neighbors, bodily functions, authority figures, clergy in some cultures but off-limits in others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the target falls within culturally legitimate categories for that audience. Consider culturally specific taboos (who is off-limits) and common targets (neighbors, bodily functions) when judging acceptability and likely reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of expression and acceptable obscenity
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultures vary in preferred modes of humor (verbal wit vs. physical comedy) and in acceptable levels of obscenity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the chosen mode aligns with cultural norms for humor and whether the level of obscenity is acceptable for the audience and occasion. A mode or obscene content that is normative in one culture may be shocking in another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public–private boundary
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural rules govern whether humor is appropriate in public versus private contexts and consider audience composition (authorities, elders, opposite sex).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine if the setting (public/private), the presence of authority figures or elders, and the gender composition affect permissibility. Some jokes are allowable only in private or within same-sex company, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status of humorists
rubrics_metrics.description: The social status of humorists (clowns, jesters, satirists) varies cross-culturally—sacred, revered, despised, or profane—and this affects how their humor is interpreted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the role/status of the performer in the culture: ritualized or official humorists may be granted licenses denied others; status shapes the function (ritual, social critique) and the audience's reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children's developmental sequence in humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Children's humor develops in a similar sequence across cultures: rhythm/repetition → incongruity → social/sexual themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this developmental sequence as a benchmark when evaluating children's humor across cultures; differences in timing or emphasis may reflect cultural socialization rather than lack of universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social function(s) of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor commonly serves three social functions across cultures: social solidarity, social control (enforcing norms), and social subversion (expressing forbidden views).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which function(s) a humorous instance is performing for that speaker–audience–context. Note that a single joke can simultaneously bind insiders, ridicule transgressors, and allow covert dissent; function influences acceptability and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-situated evaluation (funniness is not absolute)
rubrics_metrics.description: A humor instance's funniness is situated in the audience's cultural background, the relationship between speaker and target, the occasion, and the culture's taxonomy of acceptable targets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging humor, foreground the audience's cultural knowledge and expectations. Avoid assuming universal reception; instead predict likely responses by mapping audience norms, relationships, and occasion-based licenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit with theoretical accounts (incongruity/superiority/relief)
rubrics_metrics.description: Western theories (incongruity, superiority, relief) may partly explain humor cross-culturally but also reflect Western priorities; their applicability must be tested against cultural variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether an instance aligns with one of these theories, but be cautious: e.g., humor as behavioral correction (Bergson) may be salient in some cultures, while Freud's links to sexuality/aggression or Western aesthetic appreciation may not generalize. Specify which components appear universal and which are culturally contingent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic checklist for evaluating an instance
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of focused questions to diagnose acceptability and function: Is the humor occurring in a license-permitting context? Is the speaker-target relationship one where this humor is allowed? Is the target culturally legitimate? Does the humor function for solidarity, control, or subversion? What is universal vs. culturally specific in the joke's structure?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions as a practical evaluation procedure. Answer each with reference to the specific cultural norms, relationships, and occasion to reach a contextual judgment rather than an absolute one.
